Chapter.Content: 05 — Reflectance, Materials and Light Transport
Reading map · Previous chapter · Next chapter

A surface material describes how incoming energy is scattered toward outgoing directions. The chapter derives those responses, connects them to asset data, and checks mathematical properties before relying on rendered appearance.
By the end: Relate material parameters to a physically meaningful scattering model.
Recall question: Which numerical checks can reveal a broken BRDF before a scene render does?
Ask a surface where incoming energy can go
Reconstruction checkpoint — test the microfacet equations, not only the picture

tools/labs/pbr_reference_lab.cpp numerically integrates the isotropic GGX normal distribution with the projected-area measure and checks that the result stays near one for several roughness values. It checks Schlick Fresnel at normal and grazing incidence and verifies reciprocity/finiteness of the isotropic GGX + Smith reflection model for paired incoming/outgoing directions.

Those are mathematical oracles, not a complete material renderer. White-furnace energy tests, transmission, anisotropic roughness, texture/color-space decoding and glTF scene parity remain separate. Microfacet normal distributions now develops why the NDF is a projected-area density rather than a drop-in directional PDF, so later sampling/MIS derivations have the right measure from the start.

A BRDF is a bidirectional reflectance distribution function. It relates irradiance arriving from one direction to radiance leaving in another. It is not a color by itself. For a diffuse surface with reflectance , the Lambert BRDF is . The factor is the integral of the cosine over a hemisphere, so the reflected fraction remains rather than accidentally becoming .
A rough metal panel has many unresolved surface slopes. A microfacet model describes those slopes statistically. Its normal distribution function is normalized with projected area:

This is not generally the same as requiring . The probability density for sampling ordinary microfacet normals therefore includes the projected cosine. A visible-normal sampler also accounts for which facets can actually be seen from the current direction. PBRT’s microfacet derivation

In a single-scattering reflection model, Fresnel describes interface reflection, masking-shadowing describes visibility of the facets, and the familiar converts the microscopic model to a macroscopic BRDF. A perceptual roughness-to- mapping is a model convention: the convention in these examples should not silently be applied to a library that already expects .

The common metallic-roughness shader is a useful approximation, but adding -weighted Lambert diffuse to a microfacet lobe does not by itself prove exact physical layering or reciprocity. Conversely, a single-scattering rough-conductor model can lose energy because it omits repeated interreflection between facets. Use numerical integrals, documented model assumptions and controlled images together. A bright highlight alone is neither proof of energy gain nor proof of a correct BRDF: a narrow angular lobe can have values greater than one while its integrated reflectance remains bounded.
Make the asset and the shader agree

A material travels through several representations: an authored asset, a decoded CPU record, an explicitly packed GPU record, resource bindings, and the shader’s interpretation. Each transition can be correct in isolation and still disagree with the next. In glTF’s core metallic-roughness workflow, base-color RGB uses sRGB texture encoding, roughness and metallic are linear data in the green and blue channels, and alpha has its own semantics. A shader’s preferred premultiplied representation requires an explicit conversion from an asset’s straight alpha. The glTF material specification defines those asset encodings. The source below develops those contracts; general buffer ABI and descriptor-lifetime details are taught in Make a shader record an explicit binary contract.

Treat a texture index as a reference, not ownership. A recorded draw can still refer to that texture after the CPU has moved on to the next frame. The engine must retain the correct resource generation until every relevant GPU use completes. The corresponding engine lifecycle is developed in Let a renderer evolve without losing resource ownership.

Implementation-specific passages retain observations from the supplied Kairo/Maveb snapshot. They are not a fresh audit of those repositories. Source exercises and illustrative code are teaching material; only explicitly recorded checks have been executed here.

This pass covers the complete transition from “a material has some sliders” to a physically interpretable scattering model. M117 owns Parts 1945–1969: material parameters, diffuse/specular reflection, BRDF definition and constraints, Fresnel/IOR, conductor-versus-dielectric behavior, microfacet theory, GGX/Beckmann, masking-shadowing, Smith geometry, Cook–Torrance, and the denominator. M118 owns Parts 1970–1986: metallic-roughness and specular-gloss workflows, energy splitting, Disney diffuse, clearcoat, sheen, transmission, refraction, TIR, Beer–Lambert absorption, and emission.

Content.Strong: Failure modes you should now be able to diagnose

Chapter.Content: A plastic surface looks metallic even with : inspect whether baseColor has accidentally become , whether the diffuse lobe was removed, or whether dielectric is too high.
A metal looks chalky: inspect whether diffuse remains nonzero for .

A rough material becomes much darker as roughness increases: inspect microfacet multiple-scattering loss, environment prefiltering, and whether roughness is incorrectly reducing total specular amplitude instead of redistributing it.
Highlights explode into NaNs: inspect , , roughness near zero and the Cook–Torrance denominator.

Every dielectric seems to reflect exactly 4% regardless of actual optical IOR: the renderer is using the simplified metallic-roughness fixed- convention rather than an IOR-controlled dielectric model.
Glass never becomes mirror-like at grazing angles: Fresnel is missing.
Glass never exhibits TIR from inside: the refraction equation or medium transition is wrong.
Thick colored glass looks identical to thin glass: Beer–Lambert/path-length absorption is missing.
A red metal has white highlights: conductor has incorrectly been treated as neutral dielectric reflection.
A matte dielectric returns more energy than it receives: inspect whether full Lambert diffuse was added alongside full Fresnel specular without the split.
